analysis.one_liner: Restores federal tax on foreign oil profits that oil companies had stopped paying.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor bill to re-tax foreign oil income, introduced in the Senate's final days, died in the Finance Committee without a vote or a cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 Republican tax law (the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) removed a long-standing rule that taxed profits big oil companies earned through foreign subsidiaries at US rates. This bill would put that rule back, so income from foreign oil operations — like selling oil extracted abroad to customers in other countries — would again be taxed as it was before. It would apply only to large producers, exempting companies producing under 1,000 barrels a day.
analysis.who_benefits: US taxpayers, because money that oil multinationals earn abroad would again be reported and taxed in the US Treasury instead of sitting untaxed in foreign subsidiaries. Domestic producers that pay full US taxes would also face somewhat fairer competition against rivals using foreign structures.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US taxpayers and domestic taxpaying producers

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates 'foreign base company oil related income' as Subpart F income, meaning controlled foreign corporation oil income is again taxable to US shareholders rather than deferred indefinitely [S2][S3].
Applies to large producers — related groups producing 1,000 or more barrels of foreign crude oil or natural gas per day — so the burden falls on major multinationals rather than small operators [S3].
Excludes oil sold for use or consumption within the country where it was extracted, targeting profits shifted across borders rather than ordinary local sales [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational oil and gas companies and their shareholders, who would again owe current US tax on foreign oil-related income that the 2017 tax law allowed to go untaxed. Some of that cost could be passed toward consumers through prices, though the bill is designed to hit cross-border profit shifting rather than local sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large multinational oil and gas companies

drawbacks.text: The reinstated rule carves out producers under 1,000 barrels per day, leaving smaller foreign operators untaxed and creating a line that companies near the threshold have incentives to manage around [S3].

Supporters of the 2017 repeal argued the old oil-related Subpart F rules added compliance complexity and put US-based multinationals at a disadvantage against foreign competitors; restoring them reopens that debate.
Companies facing higher taxes on foreign operations could pass some of the cost to consumers through fuel prices, though the scale is uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: more federal revenue from large oil companies' foreign profits, which helps fund government services and slightly levels the field for domestic producers. The costs are modest and manageable — some compliance complexity and a possible small pass-through to prices — and the small-producer exemption limits the reach. On balance the tradeoff favors the public, but the bill as written is a narrow reinstatement, not a broad fix for offshore profit shifting.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two weeks of the Congress, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L. 115-197) repealed the provisions taxing certain foreign oil-related income as foreign base company income under Subpart F [S2].
Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced S. 3804 on December 21, 2018, to reinstate that taxation, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S3][S5].
No further action was recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large multinational oil and gas companies, which keep the untaxed treatment of foreign oil-related income that the 2017 tax law gave them, along with their shareholders.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinational oil companies and their shareholders

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate taxation of foreign oil related income and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the Congress's final days.

against.name: The oil and gas industry
against.role: Beneficiary of the 2017 repeal the bill would undo
against.what_they_did: Had no visible record of activity on this one-sponsor bill, which died without reaching a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and it never drew a recorded vote, so no partisan split can be measured; the repeal it sought to reverse had passed a Republican Congress and been signed by a Republican president in 2017.

industries.note: The bill would reinstate US tax on their foreign oil-related income, ending the carve-out created by the 2017 tax law. Their interest in keeping that carve-out runs against the public's interest in collecting the revenue, and because the bill never got a vote, they keep the current treatment.

industries.industry: Small foreign oil producers (under 1,000 barrels per day)
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts related groups producing less than 1,000 barrels of foreign oil or gas per day, so they would remain outside the tax even if it passed. The exemption narrows the revenue raised and creates an uneven line between large and small operators.
